mainTopic: Hanging the executed, why the body is taken down, the source and purpose of burial, and the purpose of a הספד.
overview: This amud opens with the last line of the משנה: the relatives of an executed person do not keep formal אבילות, but they may grieve in their hearts. The גמרא then teaches from the פסוק that the person is executed first and hung only afterward, right before sunset, and untied at once. The tree used must already be cut from the ground; רבי יוסי adds that it may not even be set back into the ground. Next the גמרא explains why the body must come down: רבי מאיר's parable of the twin king shows that a hanging body disgraces God, and אביי and רבא explain how the word קללת shows God's distress. The גמרא concludes that קללת teaches two lessons at once. It then learns from כי קבור תקברנו that leaving any dead person unburied overnight breaks a לא תעשה, and tells how King שבור asked רב חמא for a Torah source for burial. Finally the גמרא asks whether burial is for preventing disgrace or for atonement, and whether a הספד honors the living or the dead. For each question it tests several פסוקים, and every proof is turned away.

steps.title: No formal mourning, but grief in the heart
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends by saying the relatives of an executed person do not keep the outward practices of אבילות. They are still allowed to feel אנינות, private grief, because that is only in the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: The relatives would not mourn him, but they would grieve, because grief is only in the heart.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the משנה. It tells us how the family of an executed person behaves after the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה separates two things. אבילות is the outward, public set of mourning practices, and the family does not keep them. אנינות is inner sorrow, which no one can stop and which is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: keeping the outward practices of mourning (אבילות)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up אנינות here with the usual meaning of an אונן, someone whose relative has died but is not yet buried. Here it simply means private sorrow in the heart.

phrases.english: And they would not mourn,
phrases.notes: "They" means the relatives of the person who was executed.

phrases.english: but they would grieve,
since grief is only in the heart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final line of the משנה, which continues from the previous section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no formal אבילות for an executed person, but inner grief (אנינות) is allowed.

steps.title: First execution, then hanging
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows from the wording of the פסוק that the person is put to death first and hung afterward. This is unlike the government's practice of killing by hanging.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If the פסוק had only said 'a sin… and you shall hang,' I would think we hang him first and then he dies, the way the government does it. That is why the פסוק says 'and he is put to death, and you shall hang': first we kill him, then we hang him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא. It uses the order of words in the פסוק to show that hanging comes only after death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the word 'והומת,' we might have thought hanging is itself the way the person is killed, as the מלכות does. The extra word 'והומת' placed before 'ותלית' shows that death comes first, so hanging is only done to the body afterward.

keyTerms.meaning: the discussion that explains the משנה
the Sages taught (this introduces a ברייתא)

steps.whyThisMatters: It makes clear that תליה is not a way of executing someone. It is a separate act done to the body after death.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The Sages taught:
Had it said: "a sin … and you shall hang,"
phrases.notes: דברים 21:22

phrases.english: I would have said that they hang him
and afterward put him to death,
the way the government does.
The verse states: "and he is put to death, and you shall hang"

phrases.aramaic: – מְמִיתִין אוֹתוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ תּוֹלִין אוֹתוֹ.
phrases.english: so they put him to death, and afterward they hang him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא begins discussing the hanging that the משנה described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Execution comes first, and hanging comes after death, as learned from the order 'והומת ותלית.'

steps.title: How the hanging is done in practice
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains the procedure. The verdict is delayed until close to sunset, then the person is executed and hung, and right away untied, so that the body never stays up overnight.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? They wait until close to sunset, finish his judgment, put him to death, and then hang him. One person ties him and another unties him right away, just to fulfill the מצוה of hanging.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now asks how this works in practice and gives the step-by-step procedure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules must both be kept: the body must be hung, and it may not stay hanging overnight. Waiting until just before sunset and untying immediately satisfies both. The hanging is kept as short as possible, only enough to fulfill the מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: how so? (how does this work in practice)

steps.whatToRemember: The order is: delay until near sunset, finish the judgment, execute, hang briefly, and untie immediately.

phrases.english: How so?

phrases.aramaic: מְשַׁהִין אוֹתוֹ עַד סָמוּךְ לִשְׁקִיעַת הַחַמָּה,
phrases.english: They delay him until close to sunset,
and they conclude his judgment, and put him to death,
and afterward they hang him.
One ties and another unties,
in order to fulfill the מצוה of hanging.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד? מְשַׁהִין אוֹתוֹ עַד סָמוּךְ לִשְׁקִיעַת הַחַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts the rule from step 2 into practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Execute near sunset, hang the body briefly, and untie it immediately.

steps.title: The tree must already be cut from the ground
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא asks whether the עץ may be attached to the ground. From 'כי קבור' it learns that the tree, like the body, must be lacking only burial, so it must already be cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: From 'a tree,' I would think it could be either detached or attached. So the פסוק says 'you shall surely bury': it must be something that lacks only burial. This excludes a tree that still needs to be cut down and then buried.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא deals with a new question: what kind of tree is used for the hanging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'עץ' alone could include a growing tree. The phrase 'כי קבור' is read as also requiring the tree to be buried. So the tree must be in a state where burial is the only thing left to do. A growing tree would first need קציצה (cutting), so it is excluded.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: "a tree" —

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹמֵעַ אֲנִי בֵּין בְּתָלוּשׁ בֵּין בִּמְחוּבָּר.
phrases.english: I would understand either detached or attached.
The verse states: "but you shall surely bury" —
phrases.notes: דברים 21:23

phrases.english: something that is lacking only burial,
excluding this one, which is lacking cutting down and burial.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״עֵץ״ – שׁוֹמֵעַ אֲנִי בֵּין בְּתָלוּשׁ בֵּין בִּמְחוּבָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how the hanging is done to what the hanging is done on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tree must already be detached from the ground, so it lacks only burial.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: the tree may not even be stuck in the ground
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי uses the same idea to go further. A cut tree that was stuck back into the ground would need תלישה (pulling out) before burial, so it too is excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: It must be something lacking only burial. This excludes something that still needs to be pulled out and then buried.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי offers a stricter reading of the same exclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוסי, 'lacking only burial' also rules out a cut post that was set into the ground, since it would still need to be pulled out. So according to him the post must stand free, for example leaning against a wall.

keyTerms.meaning: pulling out, detaching from the ground

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
something that is lacking only burial —
excluding this one, which is lacking detaching and burial.
phrases.notes: He means a post already cut down but sunk back into the ground; it would need pulling up first.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּסָּר אֶלָּא קְבוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the רבנן of step 4 by widening their exclusion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The post may not be sunk into the ground, since it would then need תלישה before burial.

steps.title: Why the רבנן allow a post set in the ground
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן hold that pulling a cut post out of the ground is an insignificant act. Such a post therefore still counts as 'lacking only burial.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis say: pulling it out is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the רבנן respond to רבי יוסי's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree a growing tree is excluded because cutting it down is a real act. The argument is only about a post that was already cut and then set in the ground. The רבנן say pulling it out is too minor to count, so the post is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: it is nothing, it does not count

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone excludes a growing tree. The argument between רבי יוסי and the רבנן is only about a cut post set into the ground: רבי יוסי excludes it, and the רבנן say pulling it out does not count.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis:
detaching is nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the רבנן do not accept רבי יוסי's added exclusion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the minimal act (תלישה) as legally insignificant.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Perhaps a post set into the ground also lacks something besides burial.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, pulling out a cut post is nothing, so it still lacks only burial.

steps.title: The משנה's first reason: people will ask why he is hanging
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's explanation of 'כי קללת אלהים תלוי'. If the body stays up, people will ask why it is hanging, and the answer will mention that he cursed God.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is to say: 'Why is this one hanging?' 'Because he blessed [a polite word for cursed] God,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה that explains why the hanged body must come down quickly. Leaving it up keeps people talking about the blasphemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says a hanging body is 'קללת אלהים'. This reading takes it to mean that the hanging body causes God's name to be mentioned in a disgraceful way. Every passerby who asks will hear about the curse again, so the body must not stay up.

keyTerms.meaning: That he 'blessed', a polite way of saying he cursed God
Etc., the rest of the quote is assumed

phrases.english: That is to say:
Why is this one hanging?
Because he blessed, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Blessed' here is a polite way to avoid saying 'cursed God'. The משנה goes on to say God's name ends up being disgraced.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The body is taken down so that people will not keep asking about it and recalling the curse against God.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's parable of the twin brothers
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings רבי מאיר's parable. Twin brothers lived in one city, and one became king while the other became a bandit. When the bandit was hanged, people thought the king was hanging, so the king ordered him taken down.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי מאיר says, they told a parable. What is this like? It is like two twin brothers in one city. One was made king and the other became a bandit. The king commanded, and they hanged him. Everyone who saw him said, 'The king is hanging!' So the king commanded, and they took him down.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא brings a parable from רבי מאיר that explains why the hanged body is a disgrace to God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person is made in God's image, the way a twin looks just like his brother. So when a sinner hangs, it is as if God's own 'image' is hanging. That is why the King himself wants the body taken down.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whyThisMatters: This parable is the background for רבי מאיר's next statement in the משנה, that God is pained when a person is punished.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Meir says:
They told a parable,
What is the matter like?
Two twin brothers in one city.
One they appointed king,
and one went out to banditry.
The king commanded, and they hanged him.
Everyone who saw him said:
The king is hanging.
The king commanded, and they took him down.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אוֹמֵר רַבִּי מֵאִיר: מָשְׁלוּ מָשָׁל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, deeper reason for taking the body down.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because people are made in God's image, a hanging body disgraces God, so it must be taken down.

steps.title: How does רבי מאיר get 'distress' from the word 'קללת'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's line in the משנה ('קלני מראשי'). It asks how the word 'קללת' in the פסוק shows that God is in distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רבי מאיר said,' and so on. From where is this implied?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's statement from the משנה and asks how he reads it into the פסוק. This sets up the explanations of אביי and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי מאיר says God cries out 'קלני מראשי, קלני מזרועי'. The גמרא wants to know how the word 'קללת', which looks like 'curse', can mean God's pain.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the implication? How is this shown?
The word in the פסוק, simply read as 'curse of'

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir said, etc.
phrases.notes: This points to the משנה, where רבי מאיר says God cries 'קלני מראשי, קלני מזרועי': 'I am pained over My head and arm.'

phrases.english: From where is it implied?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר כּוּ׳. מַאי מַשְׁמַע
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word 'קללת' expresses God's distress.

steps.title: אביי: 'קללת' means 'I am not light'
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that קללת reads as 'קל לית', meaning 'I am not light'. In other words, God feels heavy and burdened.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is like one who says 'קל לית', 'I am not light.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by splitting the word into 'קל' (light) and 'לית' (there is not).
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this reading, God is saying 'I am not light', which means 'I feel heavy.' That heaviness is God's distress over the sinner's punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There is no lightness', meaning I feel heavy

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Like one who says, 'I am not light.'

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קללת = קל לית, 'I am not light', which means God feels heavy.

steps.title: רבא objects: then it should have said 'heavy'
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that if the meaning is 'heavy', רבי מאיר should simply have said 'כבד עלי ראשי'. He would not say 'קלני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If so, he should have said 'My head is heavy on me, my arm is heavy on me'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges אביי's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the idea is heaviness, the natural wording is 'כבד' (heavy). Saying 'קל' (light) with a hidden 'not' is a roundabout way to say it, so אביי's reading seems forced.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If so,
'My head is heavy on me,'
'My arm is heavy on me' he should have said!

steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading of קללת as 'קל לית'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the meaning is 'heavy', the wording should be כבד and not קלני.

steps.title: רבא: like saying 'the world is light for me'
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives his own explanation. 'קלני' is like the common saying 'קיל לי עלמא', 'the world is light for me'. People say 'light' as a gentle way of saying the opposite, that things feel heavy and they are in distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: It is like one who says 'קיל לי עלמא', 'the world is light for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since he rejected אביי's answer, רבא offers a different way to read the word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, 'light' is the polite word people use when they really mean 'heavy'. Someone in distress says 'the world is light for me', meaning it weighs on him. So no hidden 'not' is needed, and the wording 'קלני' fits the everyday way people speak.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The world is light for me', an expression of distress

steps.whatToRemember: אביי reads קללת as 'I am not light' (heavy). רבא reads it as the distressed saying 'the world is light for me.' Both agree it shows God's pain.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Like one who says, 'The world is light for me.'

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קללת is like 'קיל לי עלמא', a common expression of distress.

steps.title: Isn't 'קללת' needed for its plain meaning?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי מאיר can use 'קללת' for God's distress. The word is needed for its own plain lesson, that the one who curses God (the מגדף) is hanged.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this word is needed for itself!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר's דרשה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple meaning of 'קללת אלהים תלוי' is that it is the one who cursed God who gets hanged. If the word is used up teaching that law, how can it also teach God's distress?

keyTerms.meaning: For itself, for its own plain meaning
One who curses God, the blasphemer

phrases.english: Isn't this needed for itself?
phrases.notes: 'For itself' means for the plain law, that the one who curses God is hanged after being stoned.

steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's use of קללת to teach God's distress
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word is already needed to teach that the מגדף is hanged.

steps.title: If only for the law, it would say 'מקלל'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that if the פסוק came only to teach the law about the curser, it would say 'מקלל' (one who curses). The unusual word 'קללת' leaves room for רבי מאיר's lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the פסוק say 'מקלל'. Why does it say 'קללת'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to the unusual wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מקלל' would plainly mean 'a curser'. The פסוק chose 'קללת' instead, and that extra twist in the wording shows there is another lesson here, God's distress.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse say 'one who curses.'
Why 'curse of'?

steps.terutzResolutionType: Unusual wording shows an extra lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word is only for the law about the curser.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording 'קללת' instead of 'מקלל' shows it also teaches God's distress.

steps.title: Then maybe the whole פסוק is only about God's distress
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes from the other side. Perhaps the entire phrase comes only for רבי מאיר's lesson, and not to teach about hanging the curser at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that the whole thing comes for this purpose!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges the plain law, asking whether the פסוק teaches only רבי מאיר's idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the strange wording points to רבי מאיר's lesson, maybe that is its only point. Then we would have no source that the curser is the one who is hanged.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it comes for this

phrases.english: But say:
All of it comes for this purpose?

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that קללת still teaches the law of the curser
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Maybe the word teaches only God's distress and nothing about the curser.

steps.title: If only for distress, it would say 'קלת'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that if the פסוק meant only God's distress, it would say 'קלת' (lightness). The full word 'קללת' contains the idea of cursing as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the פסוק say 'קלת'. Why does it say 'קללת'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word's exact form shows it also carries the meaning of 'curse'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קלת' would mean only 'lightness'. The doubled ל in 'קללת' keeps the meaning of cursing, so the plain law about the curser is still taught.

keyTerms.meaning: Lightness, the word the פסוק would use for distress alone

phrases.english: If so, let the verse say 'lightness.'
Why 'curse of'?

steps.terutzResolutionType: The exact wording keeps both meanings
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word teaches only God's distress.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because it says 'קללת' and not 'קלת', the meaning of cursing remains.

steps.title: The word teaches two lessons
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'קללת' teaches both lessons. The curser is hanged, and God is pained when a sinner is punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion by saying the word teaches both ideas at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קללת' is neither plain 'מקלל' nor plain 'קלת'. Its blended form shows it carries both meanings: the law about hanging the מגדף and רבי מאיר's lesson of God's distress.
steps.whatToRemember: 'קללת' is a 'double' word. It is not 'מקלל' (only law) and not 'קלת' (only distress), so it teaches both.

phrases.english: Learn two things from it.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: קללת teaches both that the מגדף is hanged and that God is distressed by a sinner's punishment.

steps.title: Leaving any dead person overnight breaks a לא תעשה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that this rule applies not only to an executed person. רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי derives from 'כי קבור תקברנו' that anyone who leaves their dead unburied overnight breaks a לא תעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And not only this,' and so on. רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From where do we know that one who leaves his dead overnight transgresses a לא תעשה? The פסוק says: 'כי קבור תקברנו.' From here we learn that one who leaves his dead overnight transgresses a לא תעשה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה. That line extends the rule of quick burial to every dead person, and the גמרא gives the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק's prohibition is written about the hanged person. The doubled wording 'קבור תקברנו' widens it to every dead person. So delaying any burial overnight breaks a לא תעשה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical הלכה that a person must not delay the burial of their relative overnight without a good reason.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not only about executed criminals. The point of this line is that the prohibition covers every dead person.

phrases.english: And not only this, etc.
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: not only the executed person, but anyone who leaves his dead overnight transgresses.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
From where do we know that one who leaves his dead overnight
transgresses a prohibition because of him?
The verse teaches:
'You shall surely bury him.'
phrases.notes: דברים 21:23

phrases.english: From here, one who leaves his dead overnight
transgresses a prohibition.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא זוֹ בִּלְבַד כּוּ׳. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone who leaves their dead unburied overnight transgresses a לא תעשה, learned from 'כי קבור תקברנו'.

steps.title: A second version: the verse hints that burial itself is required
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבי יוחנן's teaching differently: 'כי קבור תקברנו' is the Torah's hint to the מצוה of קבורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Where is there a hint in the Torah to burial? The verse says, 'You shall surely bury him.' From here we have a hint to burial from the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of רבי יוחנן's teaching. In this version the verse teaches that burial itself is a Torah idea, not only that leaving the dead overnight is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 18, רבי יוחנן used this verse to teach a לא תעשה against leaving the dead unburied overnight. Here, the same verse is read as a hint that burying the dead is required in the first place. The verse stays the same, but what it teaches changes.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say: introduces a different version of a teaching
A hint: a source in the Torah that points to a law

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
From where is there a hint to burial in the Torah?
The verse says: "You shall surely bury him."
phrases.notes: דברים 21:23

phrases.english: From here there is a hint to burial from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different version of the teaching quoted in step 18, reading the same verse as a source for burial itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'כי קבור תקברנו' is the Torah's hint that the dead must be buried.

steps.title: King שבור asks רב חמא for a Torah source for burial
steps.stepSummary: שבור מלכא asks רב חמא where the Torah requires burial, and רב חמא gives no answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: King שבור said to רב חמא: Where in the Torah is burial? רב חמא was silent and said nothing to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story. A non-Jewish king asks for a Torah source for burial, and the חכם stays silent. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king's question is the same one the previous step answered: where does the Torah require burial? רב חמא's silence opens the question of why the verse from step 19 was not a good enough answer.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא לְרַב חָמָא:
phrases.english: King Shapur said to Rav Chama:
From where in the Torah is burial?

phrases.aramaic: אִישְׁתִּיק וְלָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ וְלָא מִידֵּי.
phrases.english: He was silent and did not say anything at all to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא לְרַב חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the teaching about the Torah source for burial to a story where someone is challenged to give that source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A Torah source showing that the dead must be buried.

steps.title: רב אחא בר יעקב says רב חמא should have quoted the verse
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב complains that fools run the world, since רב חמא should have answered with 'כי קבור'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב said: The world has been handed over to fools, because רב חמא should have said 'כי קבור' (you shall surely bury).
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר יעקב reacts to the story. He says the answer was easy: quote 'כי קבור'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא offers the verse from step 19 as the answer the king needed. The גמרא will now test whether this answer would really have worked against the king.

keyTerms.meaning: The world has been handed over

phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
The world has been handed over into the hands of fools,
for he should have said "for you shall surely bury."
phrases.notes: "He" is רב חמא. This answer could have been given to the king.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב: אִימְּסַר עָלְמָא בִּידָא דְּטַפְשָׁאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the king's question from step 20, which רב חמא left unanswered.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse 'כי קבור' is the Torah source for burial.

steps.title: The king could say the verse only means a coffin
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רב חמא's silence: the king could reply that 'קבור' only means to make a coffin.
steps.simpleTranslation: The king could answer: the verse means only that you should make him a coffin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב חמא. It shows how the king could have pushed away the verse רב אחא suggested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'קבור' could be read as putting the body into some container, like a coffin. If so, the verse does not prove the body must go into the ground. That is why quoting it might not have convinced the king.

keyTerms.meaning: That one should make for him

steps.confusionAlert: From here through step 32, the rejections are what King שבור could have answered. The גמרא is explaining why רב חמא stayed quiet. It is not doubting that burial is a Torah requirement.

phrases.english: That one should make him a coffin.
phrases.notes: The גמרא doesn't say who is speaking. This is what the king could have replied.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב אחא's suggested answer by showing how the king could reread the verse.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'קבור' could mean placing the body in a coffin, not in the ground.

steps.title: But the verse doubles the word: 'תקברנו'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the verse repeats the verb with 'תקברנו', so it should teach real burial.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the verse also says 'תקברנו' (bury him)!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the king's possible reply. The extra word 'תקברנו' should show that real burial is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says 'קבור תקברנו', using the verb twice. The challenge is that this doubling should add something, such as burial in the ground beyond just a coffin.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall bury him: the second, doubled form of the verb
Surely bury: the first form of the verb

phrases.english: But it says "bury him"!
phrases.notes: The verse uses the verb twice, קבור and then תקברנו. The second word is the point here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the coffin reading from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the verse only means making a coffin.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The doubled verb 'קבור תקברנו' should point to real burial.

steps.title: The king does not learn from a doubled word
steps.stepSummary: The king would not accept a lesson drawn from a doubled verb.
steps.simpleTranslation: He does not understand anything from that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the king would not accept proof from repeated words. So 'תקברנו' would not convince him either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Learning from a doubled verb is a way of reading the Torah that an outsider would not accept. To the king, the repetition would just be a style of speech. So רב חמא's silence still makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not mean anything to him: he does not learn from it

phrases.english: He does not understand anything from it.
phrases.notes: "He" is the king. He wouldn't accept a lesson drawn from a doubled word.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The proof method is not accepted by the other side.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubled verb should prove real burial even to the king.
steps.terutzMaskana: The king does not accept lessons from doubled words, so the verse would not convince him.

steps.title: Why not prove burial from the burial of the צדיקים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests רב חמא could have pointed to the burial of the righteous forefathers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let רב חמא say: we learn it from the fact that the צדיקים were buried!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a different answer רב חמא could have given. The Torah tells that the righteous forefathers were buried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since proof from words in the verse failed, the גמרא tries proof from events in the Torah. If the צדיקים were buried, burial looks like the right practice.

phrases.english: But let him say: from the fact that the righteous were buried?
phrases.notes: "Him" is רב חמא. The righteous are the forefathers buried in the Torah's stories.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the verse-based proof failed, proposes a proof from the burial of the צדיקים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He had another possible answer: the צדיקים were buried.

steps.title: That was just a custom
steps.stepSummary: The king could say the burial of the צדיקים was only the custom of the time.
steps.simpleTranslation: That was merely a custom!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the king could reject this proof. The forefathers were buried only because that was the common practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing something does not show it is commanded. The burial of the צדיקים could be a custom of their time, not a מצוה.

phrases.english: It is merely a custom!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25 by rejecting the proof from the צדיקים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: What people did does not prove a command.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The burial of the צדיקים proves burial is required.
steps.terutzMaskana: It could just be the custom of the time.

steps.title: Why not prove it from God burying משה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a stronger proof: הקדוש ברוך הוא Himself buried משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him prove it from the fact that הקדוש ברוך הוא buried משה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a stronger proof. If God Himself buried משה, burial must be the proper way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A human custom can be brushed aside, but God's own action seems more meaningful. So burial would seem to be more than just a custom.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He: God

phrases.english: From the fact that the Holy One, Blessed be He, buried Moses?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the custom answer of step 26 with an example that should not be mere custom.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that burial is only a custom.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: God's own burial of משה should show burial is more than human custom.

steps.title: God simply did not change from the custom
steps.stepSummary: The king could say God buried משה only so as not to break from the usual custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: God did it so as not to change from the custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even God burying משה could be explained as following the usual custom. The גמרא still tries two more verses (steps 29-32) before the defense of רב חמא's silence is complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: God may have buried משה in the normal way people were buried. That would not make burial a command. Every proof could be pushed away by the king, so רב חמא's silence was understandable.
steps.whatToRemember: So far every proof for burial could be rejected by the king: 'קבור' could mean a coffin, he would not learn from a doubled verb, and the burials of the צדיקים and of משה could be explained as custom. Steps 29-32 test two more verses.

phrases.english: So as not to change from the custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 27. The גמרא then tries two more verses (steps 29-32) before the defense of רב חמא's silence is complete.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains God's action as following custom, not as a command.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: God burying משה proves burial is a מצוה.
steps.terutzMaskana: God may have just kept to the usual custom, so this proves nothing to the king.

steps.title: A proof from all Israel burying אביה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a verse where all of ישראל eulogized and buried אביה, the son of ירבעם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: "And all Israel shall eulogize him and bury him."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one more proof that burial is a real obligation. It points to a verse where the whole nation buried someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the entire nation of ישראל went out to bury this person, it suggests burial is something we must do, not just a habit. This would be an answer רב חמא could have given the king, and it challenges the 'just custom' reply from steps 26-28.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source as proof

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And all Israel shall eulogize him
and bury him."
phrases.notes: מלכים א 14:13. This was said about אביה, the son of ירבעם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from משה's burial was pushed off, the גמרא tries a new verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that burial is merely a custom (steps 26-28), which justified רב חמא's silence
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A whole nation burying someone shows burial is an obligation.

steps.title: They buried him only to follow the custom
steps.stepSummary: The king could answer that they buried אביה only so as not to break from the usual custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: So as not to deviate from the custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The proof is pushed off with the same answer used before: people buried him because that is what everyone normally does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse shows that burial happened. It does not show that burial is commanded. Following a widespread custom fully explains why the nation buried him.

phrases.english: So as not to deviate from the custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof from step 29 using the same 'custom' idea as step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the event as custom rather than obligation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Burying אביה proves burial is commanded.
steps.terutzMaskana: It may have been done only to keep the common custom.

steps.title: A proof from ירמיהו's curse on the wicked
steps.stepSummary: ירמיהו cursed the wicked that they would not be buried, which suggests that normally people must be buried.
steps.simpleTranslation: "They shall not be eulogized, nor shall they be buried; they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another verse as a proof. Here the lack of burial is described as a punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If being left unburied is a curse, then being buried should be the proper and required way. The גמרא hopes this shows burial is an obligation.

phrases.english: "They shall not be eulogized, nor shall they be buried;
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 16:4. The גמרא doesn't say 'come and hear' again, but this is another attempted proof.

phrases.english: they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from אביה fails, the גמרא tries a verse about a curse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that burial is merely a custom (steps 26-30), which justified רב חמא's silence
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If not being buried is a curse, then burial must be the required norm.

steps.title: The curse was that they would be different from the custom
steps.stepSummary: The king could say the curse was only that the wicked would be cut off from the normal custom of burial.
steps.simpleTranslation: That they should deviate from the custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The proof is pushed off again: the curse means only that they would be treated differently from everyone else. That ends the attempts to find a firm proof for רב חמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being shut out of a normal custom can be a punishment even if the custom is not a מצוה. So the verse does not prove that burial is commanded. The words even mirror step 30: 'not to deviate' there, 'that they should deviate' here.
steps.whatToRemember: Every proof brought (the forefathers, משה, אביה, ירמיהו's curse) can be explained as just the custom (מנהגא). So the king could reject them all, and רב חמא had no airtight proof that burial is a מצוה.

phrases.english: That they should deviate from the custom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof from step 31 and closes the series of proofs.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the curse as exclusion from custom
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being left unburied is a curse, so burial is commanded.
steps.terutzMaskana: The curse is only being cut off from the normal custom.

steps.title: Why is burial needed: disgrace or atonement?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask whether burial is required to prevent disgrace to the dead or to bring atonement.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was asked of them: Is burial because of disgrace, or is it because of atonement?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new question about the reason behind burial.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two possible reasons. One is בזיון: leaving a body exposed is shameful. The other is כפרה: being buried brings the dead person atonement. The question is which reason the law is built on.

keyTerms.meaning: it was asked of them: an open question among the חכמים

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
Is burial because of disgrace,
or is it because of atonement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. The search for a source is over, and now the גמרא asks about the reason for burial.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the purpose of burial to prevent disgrace or to achieve atonement?

steps.title: What difference does the reason make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a practical case where the two reasons would lead to different results.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: Before trying to answer, the גמרא asks why the question matters. This sets up the next step, which gives the practical case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way, people get buried. So the גמרא wants a real-life case where the two reasons would give different rulings.

keyTerms.meaning: what practical difference comes out of this?

phrases.english: What difference does it make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical result of the question in step 33.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where 'disgrace' and 'atonement' lead to different rulings

steps.title: The case of someone who said not to bury him
steps.stepSummary: If a person asked not to be buried, the 'disgrace' reason means we ignore him. The 'atonement' reason means he gave up his own atonement. The question is left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where he said: I do not want them to bury that man. If you say burial is because of disgrace, it is not in his power to decide. And if you say it is because of atonement, he has said: I do not want atonement. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical difference: a person who said before he died that he does not want to be buried. Then it asks what the law is, and leaves the question open for now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If burial prevents disgrace, he cannot waive it, because the shame is not only his to give up. If burial is for his own atonement, it is his to give up, and he did. The final 'מאי?' means the גמרא has not yet decided which reason is correct.

keyTerms.meaning: that man: a polite way of saying 'myself'
it is not in his power

steps.confusionAlert: 'That man' (הָהוּא גַּבְרָא) is the speaker talking about himself. He is not talking about someone else.

phrases.english: Where he said:
I do not want them to bury that man.
phrases.notes: He means himself. The גמרא often says 'that man' instead of 'me' to avoid saying something bad about oneself.

phrases.english: If you say it is because of disgrace,
it is not in his power,
and if you say it is because of atonement,
he has said: I do not want atonement.
What is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר: לָא בָּעֵינָא דְּלִיקְבְּרוּהּ לְהָהוּא גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 34 with a case, then restates the open question from step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is a person who asked not to be buried. Under 'disgrace' we bury him anyway. Under 'atonement' his wish to give up atonement might be followed.

steps.title: Proof from the burial of the righteous
steps.stepSummary: צדיקים were buried, yet supposedly they need no atonement, so burial must be about preventing disgrace.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: righteous people were buried. If burial is for atonement, do righteous people need atonement?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof for the open question from Step 33. It points out that great צדיקים were buried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If burial were only for כפרה, a צדיק would not need it, because he has nothing to atone for. Since צדיקים were buried anyway, burial seems to be about preventing בזיון.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is about to bring a proof

phrases.english: Come and hear:
from the fact that the righteous were buried,
and if you say burial is because of atonement,
do the righteous need atonement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the question left open in Step 35.
steps.raayaObject: That burial is to prevent disgrace, not to bring atonement.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fact that צדיקים were buried.

steps.title: Even the righteous need atonement
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק shows that no one is completely free of sin, so even צדיקים need atonement.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, they do, as it is written: 'There is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. It says that even צדיקים need atonement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on the idea that צדיקים have no sins. The פסוק in קהלת shows that every person sins a little, so a צדיק can also be buried for כפרה.

phrases.english: Yes, as it is written:
"There is no righteous man on earth
phrases.notes: קהלת 7:20

phrases.english: who does good and never sins."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 36.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the burial of צדיקים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It wrongly assumed that צדיקים have no need for atonement.

steps.title: Proof from the burial of אביה son of ירבעם
steps.stepSummary: Only אביה was buried. If burial brings atonement, why weren't ירבעם's other sons buried too?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'All Israel will eulogize him and bury him.' If burial is so he should get atonement, the others should also be buried so they get atonement!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second proof. The navi said only ירבעם's son אביה would be buried.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If burial is for כפרה, then the wicked sons need it even more. Since they were not buried, burial seems to be about honor and disgrace, not atonement.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And all Israel will eulogize him and bury him."
phrases.notes: מלכים א 14:13, about אביה son of ירבעם.

phrases.english: And if you say
burial is so that he should get atonement,
then those should be buried too
phrases.notes: "Those" means ירבעם's other sons, who were not buried.

phrases.english: so that they should get atonement!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְסָפְדוּ לוֹ כׇל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְקָבְרוּ אֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof after the first one was rejected.
steps.raayaObject: That burial is to prevent disgrace, not to bring atonement.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א 14:13, where only אביה is buried.

steps.title: Only the righteous son deserved atonement
steps.stepSummary: אביה was righteous and was given atonement. The wicked sons were meant not to get it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one, who is righteous, should get atonement. Those ones should not get atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the second proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Burial can still be for כפרה. The wicked sons were left unburied on purpose, so that they would not get atonement.

phrases.english: This one, who is righteous,
let him get atonement;
those, let them not get atonement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 38.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed that everyone is meant to get atonement, but the wicked sons were meant to be denied it.

steps.title: Proof from ירמיהו's curse
steps.stepSummary: ירמיהו cursed the wicked not to be buried. If burial gives atonement, the wicked need it most, so burial must be about disgrace.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'They will not be eulogized and they will not be buried.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third proof, from the curse of ירמיהו. The argument is not spelled out: not burying someone sounds like a disgrace, which suggests that burial is about honor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wicked are the ones who need כפרה most. If burial were for atonement, why make it a curse to hold it back from them? This suggests that burial is about preventing בזיון.

keyTerms.meaning: And they will not be buried

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"They will not be eulogized and they will not be buried."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 16:4

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יִסָּפְדוּ וְלֹא יִקָּבֵרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third proof after two were rejected.
steps.raayaObject: That burial is to prevent disgrace.

steps.title: The curse was to deny them atonement
steps.stepSummary: The curse means: they should not get atonement. So the proof fails, and the question stays open.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that they should not get atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the third proof. The curse itself was meant to keep the wicked from getting atonement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding back burial fits the atonement reason just as well, because the punishment is losing כפרה. Since all three proofs failed, the question of בזיון or כפרה is left unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: So that there should not be

steps.whatToRemember: All three proofs (the צדיקים, ירבעם's sons, and ירמיהו's curse) can be explained either way. Whether burial is for preventing בזיון or for כפרה stays an open question.

phrases.english: so that they should not get atonement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 40.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The curse can be read as holding back atonement, not only as causing disgrace.

steps.title: Is a eulogy for the living or for the dead?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: is a הספד given to honor the living relatives or to honor the dead person?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: is a eulogy for the honor of the living, or for the honor of the dead?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question that is built like the burial question. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as burial had two possible reasons, a הספד has two possible purposes. One is honoring the family that is still alive. The other is honoring the person who died.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them

phrases.english: A question was asked among them:
Is a eulogy for the honor of the living,
or is it for the honor of the dead?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question that follows the same pattern as the burial question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose honor a הספד is for.

steps.title: What is the practical difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks in what case it would matter which reason is correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the practical difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a real case where the two reasons would give different results. This sets up the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually both the living and the dead are honored together. So the גמרא needs a case that separates the two reasons.

phrases.english: What is the practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the question in Step 42 changes in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the two reasons lead to different results.

steps.title: When the dead man asked not to be eulogized
steps.stepSummary: If the person said 'don't eulogize me,' the answer depends on whose honor the הספד is for.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where he said: 'Do not eulogize that man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first case: a person asked before he died that no הספד be given for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a הספד honors the dead, he may give up his own honor, and we listen to him. If it honors the living, he cannot give up their honor, so we still eulogize him.

keyTerms.meaning: That man (a polite way of saying 'me')

phrases.english: Where he said:
Do not eulogize that man.
phrases.notes: "That man" is a polite way of saying "me."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 43.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person who asked not to be eulogized. His request counts only if the הספד is for his own honor.

steps.title: Making the heirs pay for the eulogy
steps.stepSummary: Another difference: whether the cost of the הספד can be taken from the יורשים against their will.
steps.simpleTranslation: Alternatively: to take payment from the heirs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second case where the two reasons would matter: who pays for the הספד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a הספד honors the dead, it is his need, so it can be paid for from his estate even if the יורשים object. If it honors the living, the heirs may give up their own honor and refuse to pay.

phrases.english: Alternatively,
to take payment out from the heirs.
phrases.notes: He means making the heirs pay the eulogizer's fee from the estate, even if they don't want to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to Step 43.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Whether the cost of the הספד can be charged to the heirs against their will.

steps.title: Proof from אברהם coming to eulogize שרה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק about אברהם coming to eulogize שרה. If a הספד honors only the living, why would שרה's burial be delayed for אברהם's sake?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And אברהם came to eulogize שרה and weep over her.' If you say a הספד is for the honor of the living, would they delay שרה's burial just for אברהם's honor?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove that a הספד is for the honor of the dead, using the story of שרה's burial.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם had to come from somewhere else, so שרה's burial waited for him. Delaying a burial is normally a disgrace to the dead. If the הספד were only for אברהם's honor, it seems wrong to make שרה wait for it. So the הספד must be for her honor.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source as a proof

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And Abraham came to eulogize Sarah and to weep over her."
phrases.notes: בראשית 23:2. The word 'came' shows אברהם arrived from somewhere else, so the burial had to wait for him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשּׁוּם יְקָרָא דְּחַיֵּי הוּא,
phrases.english: And if you say it is because of the honor of the living,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם יְקָרָא דְּאַבְרָהָם מְשַׁהוּ לַהּ לְשָׂרָה?
phrases.english: would they delay Sarah's burial because of Abraham's honor?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וַיָּבֹא אַבְרָהָם לִסְפֹּד לְשָׂרָה וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the practical differences (steps 43-45), the גמרא now tries to settle the question from step 42.
steps.raayaObject: That a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 23:2: שרה's burial was delayed so that אברהם could eulogize her.

steps.title: שרה herself wanted אברהם to be honored
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: שרה herself was happy to wait so that אברהם would be honored through her.
steps.simpleTranslation: שרה herself was pleased with this, so that אברהם would be honored through her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns away the proof from שרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the הספד is for the honor of the living, the delay was not a disgrace to שרה. She herself wanted אברהם to have the honor of eulogizing her. So the פסוק fits both sides, and nothing is proven.

keyTerms.meaning: it is pleasing to her, she is happy with it

phrases.english: Sarah herself was pleased with it,
so that Abraham would be honored through her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 46.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. The question from step 42 stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The delay was no disgrace, because שרה herself wanted אברהם to be honored.

steps.title: Proof from the הספד for ירבעם's son
steps.stepSummary: All Israel eulogized the son of ירבעם. If the הספד honors the living, would his wicked family deserve that honor?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And all Israel shall eulogize him and bury him.' If you say a הספד is for the honor of the living, are those people worthy of honor?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second proof that a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son of ירבעם was given a הספד by all Israel. His living family was wicked and did not deserve honor. So the הספד must have been for the son's own honor.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And all Israel shall eulogize him and bury him."
phrases.notes: מלכים א 14:13. This is said about אביה, the son of ירבעם.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשּׁוּם יְקָרָא דְּחַיֵּי הוּא,
phrases.english: And if you say it is because of the honor of the living,
are those people worthy of honor?
phrases.notes: 'Those people' means ירבעם's family, the living relatives, who were wicked.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וְסָפְדוּ לוֹ כׇל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְקָבְרוּ אֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new attempt to prove the same point, after the first proof was rejected.
steps.raayaObject: That a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א 14:13: the son of ירבעם was eulogized even though his family was wicked.

steps.title: The righteous are happy when others are honored through them
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: a צדיק is happy for people to be honored through him, even unworthy relatives.
steps.simpleTranslation: The righteous are pleased that people are honored through them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns away the proof from ירבעם's son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son was a צדיק, and a צדיק wants others to gain honor through him. So even if the הספד honors the living, it makes sense to give it, because the dead son would want that. The פסוק proves nothing.

phrases.english: It is pleasing to the righteous
that people are honored through them.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִיחָא לְהוּ לְצַדִּיקַיָּא דְּמִיַּיקְּרִי בְּהוּ אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 48.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. The question stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dead צדיק's own wish explains why his unworthy relatives received the honor.

steps.title: Proof from the curse that the wicked will not be eulogized
steps.stepSummary: The wicked are cursed that they will have no הספד. If a הספד honors the living, why take it away when they may have righteous relatives?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'They shall not be eulogized, nor shall they be buried.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third proof, but it only quotes the פסוק and leaves the question unspoken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the הספד honors the living, a wicked person with righteous relatives should still get one for their sake. The curse takes away the הספד completely. That suggests the הספד is about the dead person, who does not deserve honor.

keyTerms.meaning: and they shall not be buried

steps.confusionAlert: The question here is not written out. The גמרא expects you to supply it: 'If a הספד is for the living, why should the righteous relatives lose it?'

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"They shall not be eulogized, nor shall they be buried."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 16:4. The question is left unsaid: if the הספד is for the living, why deny it to righteous relatives?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: לֹא יִסָּפְדוּ וְלֹא יִקָּבֵרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third attempt to settle the question.
steps.raayaObject: That a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 16:4: the wicked are denied a הספד, even though their relatives might deserve honor.

steps.title: The righteous do not want honor through the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: righteous relatives do not want to be honored through a wicked person.
steps.simpleTranslation: The righteous are not pleased to be honored through the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns away the third proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the הספד honors the living, righteous relatives would refuse honor that comes through a רשע. So there is nobody who wants the הספד, and it is not given. The curse fits both sides.

phrases.english: It is not pleasing to the righteous
to be honored through the wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 50. It mirrors the idea of step 49 in reverse.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. The question stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The righteous relatives themselves don't want honor that comes through a רשע.

steps.title: Proof from the promise to צדקיהו
steps.stepSummary: ירמיהו promised צדקיהו that he would be eulogized like the kings before him. If a הספד only honors the living, what does צדקיהו gain from that promise?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'You shall die in peace, and like the burnings for your fathers, the earlier kings before you, so they will burn for you, and they will eulogize you, saying "Ah, master!"' If you say a הספד is for the honor of the living, what does he gain from it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a fourth proof that a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירמיהו gives צדקיהו a הספד as a comfort and a promise. A promise only makes sense if צדקיהו himself benefits. So it seems the הספד is for the dead person's honor.

keyTerms.meaning: burnings (done in honor of the kings at their funerals)
what does he gain from it?

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"You shall die in peace;
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 34:5. ירמיהו is speaking to צדקיהו, the king.

phrases.english: and with the burnings of your fathers, the former kings

phrases.aramaic: אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לְפָנֶיךָ כֵּן יִשְׂרְפוּ לָךְ
phrases.english: who were before you, so shall they burn for you;
and 'Ah, master!' they will eulogize you."

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשּׁוּם יְקָרָא דְּחָיֵי הוּא,
phrases.english: And if you say it is because of the honor of the living,
what does he gain from it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בְּשָׁלוֹם תָּמוּת וּבְמִשְׂרְפוֹת אֲבוֹתֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth attempt to settle the question.
steps.raayaObject: That a הספד is for the honor of the dead.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 34:5: a הספד is promised to צדקיהו as a personal comfort.

steps.title: The promise was that Israel would be honored through him
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: ירמיהו meant that Israel would be honored through צדקיהו, just as they were honored through his fathers.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he was telling him: Israel will be honored through you, just as they were honored through your fathers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns away the fourth proof by reading ירמיהו's promise differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the הספד honors the living, צדקיהו can still be comforted. He would know that the people will gain honor through him, the way they did through the earlier kings. So none of the four proofs settles the question.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what he was saying to him

steps.whatToRemember: All four proofs (שרה, ירבעם's son, the wicked, צדקיהו) can be explained either way. The question of whose honor a הספד is for is not settled by these פסוקים.

phrases.english: This is what he was saying to him:
Israel will be honored through you
just as they were honored through your fathers.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר לֵיהּ: לִיַּיקְּרוּ בָּיךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 52.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. The question stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The promise can mean that צדקיהו's comfort is knowing that Israel will be honored through him.
